主要内容: The U.S. Department of the Treasury, along with the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), has made financial inclusion a key policy priority, resulting in significant progress over the past eight years. In the United States, the unbanked rate fell by 15 percent between 2011 and 2015, reaching a historic low of 7 percent. Globally, the number of adults without access to formal financial services dropped by 20 percent from 2.5 billion to 2.0 billion between 2011 and 2014. These gains were driven by strong partnerships among governments, private sector actors, and nonprofits. New technologies, such as mobile phones and the Internet, have further expanded opportunities to bring more people into the formal financial system. Four new initiatives were announced to build on this progress, including the Financial Inclusion Fellows program, India’s first cashless city, the Digital Development Advisor Program, and an updated National Strategy for Financial Literacy. The administration has also invested in community development financial institutions (CDFIs), which have expanded services to 43,000 consumers and made 58,000 small-dollar loans. The CDFI Program invested $1.1 billion over six years, contributing to over $14 billion in loans and investments. The initiative also prioritized financial inclusion in global forums like the G-20 and launched myRA, a retirement savings account for those without employer-sponsored plans. The Barcelona Principles were established to ensure humanitarian cash aid via digital payments supports long-term recovery. The Office of Technical Assistance (OTA) is working in eight countries to develop financial inclusion strategies and modernize financial infrastructure. In 2016, CDFI awardees provided 23,000 small-dollar loans and opened 3,741 Individual Development Accounts. USAID supported cash preparedness through grants to Mercy Corps and CRS, focusing on digital cash transfers. The Financial Empowerment Innovation Fund invested $6.2 million in research to improve financial health. The Better than Cash Alliance (BTCA), co-founded by USAID, now includes 24 national governments and other organizations. USAID also made e-payments the default method for development assistance, leading to significant efficiency gains in Bangladesh. The RegTech for Regulators Accelerator and MyMoneyAppUp Challenge further promoted digital innovation and financial empowerment. The U.S. Department of the Treasury highlighted eight years of progress on financial inclusion, emphasizing the role of private and public sector mentors in supporting entrepreneurs. Over 250 mentors participated in helping these entrepreneurs develop and scale their businesses, with the infusion of investment capital and expertise aiding the growth of early-stage financial services companies. These efforts aim to bring financial innovations to customers and communities globally. Additionally, the Coca-Cola System contributed $1 million to Operation HOPE in the past year to support financial literacy, career training, and entrepreneurship programs. This initiative has already benefited over 31,662 women and girls in the United States, with plans to educate 192,000 through classroom and digital programs by 2019.
